passage: When Ganpat kaka died suddenly in the fields, the whole village of Wadgaon crowded into his courtyard. People said the right words, touched Preeti kaki's feet and left. Vaibhav, who lived two houses down, didn't know what to say, so he didn't say much. He brought a pot of dal and rice every evening for a week. He milked their two buffaloes at dawn, since nobody else remembered them. When Preeti kaki wanted to talk about how Ganpat kaka hummed while tying his turban, Vaibhav sat on the step and listened, sometimes for an hour. On the tenth day she said, 'Everyone gave me advice. You gave me milk and dal and your ears.' Vaibhav looked down, embarrassed, and went to check the buffaloes.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav bring every evening for a week?
qa.a: A pot of dal and rice.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about not knowing what to say?
qa.a: He felt awkward and unsure with words, so he chose practical help instead.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's actions mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Milking the forgotten buffaloes and listening on the step; practical help and presence meant more than advice.

qa.q: How did Preeti kaki experience the villagers' visits compared with Vaibhav's help?
qa.a: The visits brought words and advice that didn't help much, while Vaibhav's food, work and listening made her feel truly supported.

grounding: A young man supports a bereaved neighbour through food, practical tasks and listening rather than perfect words.

passage: When Kofi's mother died, the whole office in Manchester signed a big card. Soo-ah signed it too, but it felt too small. She remembered that when her own grandmother died, what she had needed most was someone to take care of dinners. So she started a meal rota and asked eight colleagues to cover one evening each. She dropped off a pot of spiced rice with a note that just said, 'No need to reply.' At the funeral she didn't try to give a speech; she stood at the back and stacked chairs afterwards. Two weeks later, Kofi came back to work and stopped by her desk. 'I didn't eat properly for days. Then the food started arriving. Thank you.'

qa.q: How many colleagues did Soo-ah ask to join the meal rota?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: Why did the card feel too small to Soo-ah?
qa.a: She felt it wasn't enough, remembering that when her grandmother died she had most needed practical help with dinners.

qa.q: What made Soo-ah's help useful?
qa.a: Organising regular meals, adding a 'No need to reply' note, and helping quietly at the funeral instead of making speeches.

qa.q: How did the arriving food feel for Kofi?
qa.a: He hadn't been eating properly for days, so the meals likely felt like real care and relief.

grounding: A colleague supports a grieving co-worker with a meal rota and quiet presence rather than words.

passage: The morning after Naveen's father died, the badminton group at the community centre didn't play. Yash, who organised the Sunday games, made a list on the back of a score sheet: who could drive relatives from the station, who could bring tiffin, who could set up chairs for the prayer meeting. Nobody made a speech. Twelve names went down in twenty minutes. At the prayer meeting, Yash didn't try to find perfect words for Naveen. He just stood beside him while people came and went, and handed him water when his voice cracked. Later that week, when Naveen came back to the centre for the first time, the group played doubles as usual, and Yash made sure Naveen was on his side.

qa.q: What did Yash write the list on?
qa.a: The back of a score sheet.

qa.q: What might Naveen have felt when he came back and found the usual doubles game?
qa.a: Likely relieved and comforted, welcomed back to something normal without fuss.

qa.q: How did Yash turn the group's sympathy into real help?
qa.a: By listing practical tasks, like station pick-ups, tiffins and chairs, so twelve people could each do something useful.

qa.q: What was it like for the badminton group to be given specific tasks?
qa.a: They could act on their sadness instead of feeling helpless, which is why twelve names went down so quickly.

grounding: A community group supports a bereaved member through presence and practical tasks rather than perfect words.

passage: Nanny's note for Nazia, Tuesday. Vasudha fought her nap again until I did it your way: curtains, then the blue blanket, then 'Chanda mama' twice. By the second song she was sucking her thumb and holding the blanket corner. She was asleep before 1:30. At lunch she refused rice until I put it in her own steel bowl with the elephant. Will keep the same order tomorrow 🙂

qa.q: Which song did the nanny sing twice?
qa.a: 'Chanda mama'.

qa.q: What does Vasudha holding the blanket corner and sucking her thumb suggest?
qa.a: She was feeling calm and safe once the familiar order of curtains, blanket and song was followed.

qa.q: What is the nanny planning, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the same order tomorrow, because Vasudha settles when each step is predictable.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel reading the note?
qa.a: Likely relieved and pleased that Nazia's routine works even when Nazia is away, so Vasudha feels at home with the nanny too.

grounding: A toddler settles for sleep and meals when the same familiar sequence is followed.

passage: In their village house, dinner always went the same way for little Yash. Aaji rang the brass bell at the tulsi, everyone sat on the floor, and Yash climbed into his sister Nandini's lap. One ball of dal-rice for the cow, one for the crow, one for Yash. One night Nandini was away at a wedding, and Yash cried and pushed his plate away. Aaji rang the bell. He stopped, watched, and opened his mouth for the crow's bite.

qa.q: Where did Yash usually sit at dinner?
qa.a: In his sister Nandini's lap.

qa.q: Why did Yash cry and push his plate away?
qa.a: He felt upset and unsettled because Nandini was away and the usual dinner order was broken.

qa.q: What did Aaji do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She rang the brass bell, a familiar first step, which told Yash dinner was happening the usual, safe way.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel hearing about that night?
qa.a: She might feel touched that her part mattered so much, and glad Aaji knew how to keep the routine going.

grounding: A toddler relies on a familiar mealtime sequence, and a familiar step helps him settle when part of it changes.

passage: Every night in their flat in Lagos, Ada's bedtime went in the same order: bath, pyjamas with stars, then Mummy Nkechi's song about the sleeping moon, while Daddy switched off the big light and her brother Chidera whispered 'Goodnight, Ada' from the top bunk. The night the power went out, everything was dark and wrong. Ada wailed. Mummy lit a lamp and sang the moon song anyway. Chidera whispered his line. Ada's sobs slowed. She tucked her toy rabbit under her chin and closed her eyes.

qa.q: What did Ada tuck under her chin?
qa.a: Her toy rabbit.

qa.q: Why did Ada wail when the power went out?
qa.a: She was frightened and unsettled because the dark changed the usual bedtime order.

qa.q: What helped Ada settle, even in the dark?
qa.a: Mummy Nkechi singing the same moon song and Chidera whispering his line, so the routine stayed the same.

qa.q: How might Chidera feel whispering his line in the dark?
qa.a: He may feel proud and grown-up, helping calm his little sister with his part of the routine.

grounding: A toddler settles at bedtime through the same family sequence, even when the power goes out.

passage: On Lucia morning in Uppsala, Jin woke before it was light. Mormor Ulla helped him into a long white shirt and gave him a paper star on a stick. Mamma, Pappa and his cousins lined up in the dark hallway. Jin held his star very straight and walked slowly, singing the only words he knew, 'Sankta Lucia', loud and proud. When they reached Morfar's room with the saffron buns, Morfar clapped. Jin whispered to Mormor, 'Did I do it right?' She nodded, and he beamed.

qa.q: What did Mormor Ulla give Jin to hold?
qa.a: A paper star on a stick.

qa.q: What does Jin asking 'Did I do it right?' show?
qa.a: He wanted very much to do the custom properly and felt proud and delighted to be part of it.

qa.q: How did the family help Jin join the tradition?
qa.a: Mormor dressed him, gave him a star and a place in the line, and nodded when he asked, so he felt he belonged.

qa.q: How might Morfar feel watching Jin in the procession?
qa.a: Likely happy and touched to see his grandson join the family's Lucia morning.

grounding: A young child joins a family festival custom and delights in doing it right.

passage: At the playschool's Diwali morning, Pallavi ma'am showed the children how to light a diya: hold it steady, let the teacher bring the matchstick, keep fingers away from the flame. Eshaan held his clay diya with both hands like a baby bird. 'Like Dadi does it!' he said. When the flame caught, he gasped and looked at his friends. Mehul and Anu had theirs lit too. Eshaan carefully placed his in the row on the rangoli and folded his hands, eyes shut tight, just like at home.

qa.q: Who brought the matchstick to light the diyas?
qa.a: The teacher, Pallavi ma'am.

qa.q: What does Eshaan saying 'Like Dadi does it!' suggest?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, happy to be doing the custom the way his family does.

qa.q: How did Pallavi ma'am make the custom safe and joyful?
qa.a: She showed each step clearly, lit the diyas herself, and let the children place them and pray in their own way.

qa.q: What might Mehul and Anu feel with their own diyas lit beside Eshaan's?
qa.a: They probably shared the excitement, so the row of lights felt like something the whole group did together.

grounding: A young child joins a festival custom at school and delights in doing it the way the family does.

passage: Saturday: Bidisha watched Pallavi pishi draw alpana on the floor with rice paste, swirling tiny feet all the way from the door. 'Lakshmi's footsteps,' pishi said. Bidisha tried one and made a blob. She frowned. Sunday: she practised on the balcony with chalk, tongue poking out, making little feet over and over. Tuesday, puja day: pishi handed her the bowl. Bidisha drew three wobbly feet near the door, all by herself. Thamma smiled and said, 'Now Lakshmi will come to our house.' Bidisha stood in the doorway all evening, guarding her footprints.

qa.q: What did Pallavi pishi draw with rice paste?
qa.a: Alpana, with tiny feet from the door: Lakshmi's footsteps.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel on puja day after drawing the feet?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, guarding her footprints all evening after Thamma's words.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha learn the custom?
qa.a: Watching pishi, practising with chalk on her own, and then being trusted with the bowl on puja day.

qa.q: How might Pallavi pishi feel seeing Bidisha's wobbly feet?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and warm, seeing the tradition passed on to the next child.

grounding: Over several days a young child learns a family festival custom and delights in doing it right.

passage: Monday: under the stairs at school, Ujjwal, Keerthana and Manav invented the Tiger Club. The handshake was two slaps, a fist bump and a growl. Rule one: nobody tells the password. Ujjwal felt ten feet tall. Thursday: a new boy, Arif, asked to join. Keerthana said, 'Tiger Club is only three.' Arif walked off, and Ujjwal felt a strange mix of pride and guilt. The next Monday: Ujjwal saw Arif eating alone again. At the stairs, Ujjwal said, 'What if we had a joining test? Like, he has to growl.' Manav rolled his eyes but agreed. Arif growled so loudly that a teacher looked round. The Tiger Club was four.

qa.q: What was the Tiger Club handshake?
qa.a: Two slaps, a fist bump and a growl.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Arif walked off on Thursday?
qa.a: A strange mix of pride in the club and guilt at shutting Arif out.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do to let Arif in, and why did it work?
qa.a: Suggested a joining test, a growl, so Arif could belong without the club losing its special ritual.

qa.q: What was it like for Arif to be turned away and then let in?
qa.a: He likely felt rejected and lonely at first, then happy and accepted, growling loud enough for a teacher to look round.

grounding: Children invent a club ritual that marks who belongs, and later stretch it to include a newcomer.

passage: Parul, you and your friends have a secret handshake? Your Thomas uncle had one too, in Kottayam, sixty years ago. Five of us, the Mango Tree Gang. To join, you had to climb to the third branch and eat a raw mango without making a face. Our sign was two taps on the nose. We thought we were kings. Then a boy called Varghese moved into our street. He couldn't climb because of his leg brace. We said rules are rules. For a whole summer he watched us from his gate. One evening I climbed down and brought him a mango. I tapped my nose twice. The others were angry for a day. After that, the rule was: climb or be carried. Remember that when you make your rules.

qa.q: What was the Mango Tree Gang's sign?
qa.a: Two taps on the nose.

qa.q: How might Varghese have felt watching from his gate all summer?
qa.a: Probably lonely and left out, shut out by a rule he couldn't meet.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed the gang, and why?
qa.a: Young Thomas bringing Varghese a mango and giving him the sign; it showed the ritual could welcome, not only exclude.

qa.q: How did the other gang members react to the new rule?
qa.a: They were angry for a day, protective of their rules, but then accepted 'climb or be carried'.

grounding: An uncle recalls a childhood gang whose joining ritual marked who belonged, until he stretched it to include a boy left out.

passage: The Secret Stitchers had one rule: every Saturday at four, under the jamun tree behind Block C, each member showed one thing she had sewn, and they all said, 'Needle, thread, friends ahead!' This Saturday it poured. The tree was dripping, and Sharmila's mother wouldn't let four muddy girls into the flat. Simran looked ready to cry; the club had never missed a week. Then Sharmila had an idea: the staircase landing. They squeezed in between the fourth and fifth floors, knees touching, and showed their pieces: a pencil pouch, a crooked heart, a doll's scarf. The lift man peered at them. They whispered the chant so nobody else would hear, which made it feel even more secret and even better.

qa.q: Where did the Secret Stitchers usually meet?
qa.a: Under the jamun tree behind Block C.

qa.q: Why did Simran look ready to cry?
qa.a: She was upset and worried because the rain threatened to make the club miss a week for the first time.

qa.q: How did Sharmila keep the ritual going despite the rain?
qa.a: By finding the staircase landing, so they could still show their pieces and say the chant together.

qa.q: How might the lift man see the four girls on the landing?
qa.a: He probably found them puzzling or amusing, not knowing the whispered chant marked who belonged to their club.

grounding: Children keep their club's made-up ritual going through bad weather, because it marks who belongs.

passage: Rajni, you asked why I was so quiet at the Shraadh lunch. Okay, Akash's honest version. Every year we feed the crows and the priest for my great-grandparents, and this year I asked Papa, 'Do you really think the food reaches them?' The whole table went silent. My chacha said I'd become too clever from the internet. Papa didn't get angry. He said, 'I don't know if it reaches them. I know it reaches me. It's how I remember my dadi.' That stayed with me. I still don't believe the crows are carrying food anywhere. But I love Papa, and I saw his face when he set the plate out. So I helped. I just don't know yet what I believe, and I think that's allowed.

qa.q: What did Akash ask Papa at the Shraadh lunch?
qa.a: 'Do you really think the food reaches them?'

qa.q: How did Akash feel after Papa's answer?
qa.a: Akash felt moved and torn, still not believing the food reaches anyone but loving Papa and seeing what the ritual means to him.

qa.q: What made Akash's questioning respectful?
qa.a: Asking honestly, listening to Papa's answer, and still helping with the plate while working out personal beliefs.

qa.q: How might Papa see Akash's question?
qa.a: He took it calmly and answered honestly, treating it as a real question, since for him the ritual is about remembering his dadi.

grounding: A teenager questions a family ritual, feeling both love for the family and a wish to own personal beliefs.

passage: Monday: at dinner Dadaji announced the family's yearly barefoot walk to the hill temple. Lalit put down his spoon. 'Why barefoot? God can't want our feet to bleed.' His cousin Irawati kicked him under the table, then whispered, 'I've wondered too.' Wednesday: Lalit asked Dadaji again, politely this time, while helping him water the plants. Dadaji said his own father first walked it after a bad harvest year, to say thank you. 'You don't have to believe what I believe. Just know why we do it.' Saturday: Lalit walked up the hill with the family, in thin cotton socks. He didn't pray the way Dadaji did, but at the top he stood beside him, quiet, and watched him fold his hands.

qa.q: What did Lalit wear on the walk?
qa.a: Thin cotton socks.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling at the top of the hill?
qa.a: Lalit felt quietly respectful and a little moved, not sharing Dadaji's prayer but wanting to stand beside him.

qa.q: What helped Lalit move from challenge to understanding?
qa.a: Asking again politely, one to one while helping Dadaji, and listening to the story behind the walk.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about Lalit's questions?
qa.a: She has the same doubts, so she's partly relieved someone asked, even though she kicked him to avoid a scene at dinner.

grounding: Over a week a teenager questions a family ritual respectfully and finds a way to take part without full belief.

passage: Raghav, you think you're the first teenager in this family to doubt the fasts? Your Kalyani paati was worse. At fifteen I refused to fast on Ekadashi. I said, 'If God is love, why does love need hunger?' My mother cried, and my grandmother didn't speak to me for two days. I felt awful. I loved them, and I also couldn't pretend. Then my grandmother called me to the kitchen and said, 'Don't fast, then. But sit with me while I cook for the evening, and ask me your questions.' So every Ekadashi I sat there, asking and arguing, while she explained what her mother had told her. I still don't fast. But I know every story, and now I tell them to you.

qa.q: On which day did young Kalyani refuse to fast?
qa.a: On Ekadashi.

qa.q: How did young Kalyani feel when the grandmother stopped speaking for two days?
qa.a: She felt awful and torn, loving her family but unable to pretend to believe.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped both sides?
qa.a: The grandmother inviting Kalyani to sit and ask questions while she cooked, so Kalyani could stay close without pretending.

qa.q: How might the grandmother have felt when young Kalyani refused?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and worried at first, then chose to keep her granddaughter close through questions and stories.

grounding: A grandmother recalls questioning a family fast as a teenager and how respectful questions kept her close to her family.

passage: Last year I'd have quit the colony's Ganesh mandal. The older boys wanted a DJ blasting till midnight, and I hate that noise; our neighbour's baby cried every night. Everyone else said yes. I said no, out loud, in the meeting. It was awkward. Someone called me 'uncle'. But Ishita, who runs the decorations, said, 'Madhav's allowed to think that. Can he still help with the lights?' And I did. I stayed till two in the morning wiring the pandal, and I laughed with the same boys who'd teased me. I didn't change my mind about the DJ. They didn't change theirs. We ended up agreeing on ten o'clock. I'm still one of them, just a slightly quieter one.

qa.q: What did Madhav help with at the pandal?
qa.a: Wiring the lights, till two in the morning.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel after speaking against the DJ?
qa.a: He felt awkward and exposed, especially when teased, but still wanted to stay part of the mandal.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helped the group allow difference?
qa.a: She said Madhav was allowed his view and invited him to keep helping, showing that disagreeing didn't mean leaving.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Madhav by the end?
qa.a: They teased him at first, but after he worked till two and laughed with them, they likely saw him as still one of them, just with a different view.

grounding: A teenager keeps belonging to a community group while holding a different view, and the group makes room for it.

passage: Youth club leader's note, Sunday. Simran joined the football team in June and fitted in quickly. This week the team started a pre-match chant that mocks the other side's town. Simran didn't join in; she just clapped for our own players. A few teammates asked if she thought she was better than them. She said, 'No. I just cheer for us, not against them.' Rafiq, the captain, backed her: 'She's on the team. That's what matters.' I spoke to the team afterwards and said I was glad someone could belong here without copying everyone, and that good teams have room for that. Simran scored in the second half, and the whole bench mobbed her. Next week I will ask the team to write a new chant together.

qa.q: What did Simran say when asked if she thought she was better?
qa.a: 'No. I just cheer for us, not against them.'

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when teammates questioned her?
qa.a: She was probably uncomfortable and a little anxious about being seen as superior, yet steady enough to explain calmly.

qa.q: What did the leader do to help the team make room for difference?
qa.a: Told the team that belonging doesn't require copying everyone, and planned for them to write a new chant together.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq have backed Simran?
qa.a: As captain, Rafiq values the team over sameness, and may have seen that her way still supported the team.

grounding: A youth leader's note on a teenager who belongs to a team while quietly not joining a mocking chant.

passage:
Diary, Friday.
Our group decided the science fair is 'for nerds' and nobody's entering. Elizabeth said it first, and everyone nodded. I didn't say anything, but I'd already started my water-filter model, and honestly I love it.
Today I told them I'm entering anyway. Silence. Then Aditi said, 'So you're a nerd now?' I laughed and said, 'Always was. You just didn't notice.'
I was scared they'd drop me from lunch. They didn't. Elizabeth even asked how the filter works, and at the end she said, 'Okay, fine, we'll come and clap.'
I'm still in the group. I'm just the one with the filter.
Keerthana

qa.q: What model had Keerthana started?
qa.a: A water-filter model.

qa.q: What was Keerthana afraid of before telling the group?
qa.a: Keerthana was scared of being dropped from the lunch group for going against their decision.

qa.q: What in Keerthana's approach helped keep both the friendship and the choice?
qa.a: Saying it lightly with a joke, not attacking the group's view, and staying at lunch as usual.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth's view seem to shift?
qa.a: She started the 'for nerds' idea but then asked how the filter works and promised to come and clap, showing the group could hold a difference.

grounding: A teenager stays in a friend group while making a different choice, and the group turns out to allow it.

passage: Avni, before you go to the hostel, let your Anirban mama tell you something. In my first week of engineering college, the seniors called us freshers up to the terrace at midnight. They said joining the 'family' meant doing whatever they asked. First it was singing, which was silly but fine. Then they told my roommate Pradeep to take off his shirt and stand in the cold. I wanted so badly to belong that I almost laughed along. Pradeep was shaking. Something in me said no. I walked him down the stairs, and the next morning we went together to the warden and the anti-ragging committee. The seniors were suspended. For a month some people wouldn't talk to us. Then others started saying thank you. Belonging that needs someone humiliated isn't belonging.

qa.q: Where did the seniors call the freshers at midnight?
qa.a: Up to the terrace.

qa.q: Why did young Anirban almost laugh along?
qa.a: He wanted so badly to belong that going along felt safer than standing out, even while he was uneasy.

qa.q: Which choice in the story was the turning point, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Walking Pradeep down and reporting to the warden and anti-ragging committee the next morning; it stopped the harm and protected others.

qa.q: What was it like for Pradeep on the terrace?
qa.a: Pradeep was shaking and humiliated, likely frightened and powerless in front of the seniors.

grounding: An uncle recalls how the wish to belong nearly led him to accept a humiliating initiation, until he protected his roommate and reported it.

passage: Sarika had been in Pune for nine days, knew nobody, and her phone was broken, so she couldn't even call home. The college dance society was the first place that felt friendly. Then the seniors said new members had to 'earn their place': wash the seniors' practice clothes, stay silent at meals, and never tell the teachers. Two other first-years did it without complaint. Sarika scrubbed a pile of T-shirts in the hostel bathroom till midnight, telling herself this was belonging. The next day her classmate Uday saw her raw hands. 'That's ragging,' he said quietly. 'You don't have to earn a club.' That afternoon they went together to the society's faculty adviser, who called the seniors in the same day, ended the 'tasks' and told Sarika she was welcome at practice.

qa.q: How long had Sarika been in Pune?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: Why did Sarika keep scrubbing till midnight?
qa.a: She was lonely and desperate to belong, with no phone to call home, so she told herself the tasks were part of joining.

qa.q: What made Uday's response helpful?
qa.a: He named it as ragging, said she didn't have to earn a club, and went with her to the faculty adviser the same day.

qa.q: How might the two first-years who did the tasks without complaint be feeling?
qa.a: They may also feel humiliated but afraid of losing their place, and relieved when the adviser ended the tasks.

grounding: A lonely new student accepts humiliating tasks to belong until a classmate names it and an adult ends it the same day.

passage: In his second week at a Delhi college, Hrithik was told by the cricket team's seniors that every fresher had to ride the metro wearing a cardboard sign saying 'I AM A DONKEY' and bray at each station. The other freshers laughed nervously. Hrithik's stomach dropped, but he wanted the team so badly that he picked up the marker. Mohit, a second-year player, walked in. 'No. We're not doing this anymore.' A senior argued, 'It's tradition, it builds bonding.' Mohit said, 'Then let's bond at a five a.m. run at the stadium. All of us, seniors too.' Grumbling, they agreed. The next morning, twelve players ran laps in the dark, freshers and seniors panting together. Hrithik still told the sports teacher about the sign, and a no-ragging rule went up on the notice board.

qa.q: What did the sign say?
qa.a: 'I AM A DONKEY'.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he picked up the marker?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he felt humiliated and anxious, but wanted to join the team so badly that he nearly went along.

qa.q: How did Mohit keep the bonding but remove the harm?
qa.a: He refused the humiliating task and replaced it with a five a.m. run for everyone, seniors too, so the shared effort had no victim.

qa.q: How might the senior who called it tradition feel?
qa.a: Probably annoyed and defensive at first, but running laps with the freshers may show that bonding doesn't need humiliation.

grounding: A new student is pushed toward a humiliating initiation; a senior replaces it with shared hardship without harm, and a teacher is told.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Tejas, you asked why I make appam in a rice cooker every Sunday. Jomon's confession: I'm homesick. At home in Thrissur, Sunday means church at seven, then Ammachi's appam and stew, then everyone fighting over the newspaper. Here in the Delhi hostel, Sunday is just a longer Saturday. My first month, I slept till noon and felt empty, and didn't even know why. Then one Sunday I smelled coconut in the canteen and nearly cried. So I bought a small rice cooker, begged Amma for the batter recipe on a voice call, and started making wobbly appams at eight. Now you and two others turn up with plates. It's not home. But it's a Sunday again.

qa.q: What does Jomon make every Sunday?
qa.a: Appam, in a rice cooker.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling during the first month in the hostel?
qa.a: Jomon felt homesick and empty, sleeping till noon on Sundays without knowing why.

qa.q: What did Jomon do to feel anchored again?
qa.a: Created a small new ritual, making appams every Sunday at eight, and let friends join in.

qa.q: What might Sunday appams mean to Tejas and the two others?
qa.a: A warm shared breakfast that may give them their own small weekly anchor in the hostel too.

grounding: A young person in a hostel misses home's small rituals and builds a new weekly one to feel anchored.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: October 20: Hansa woke in her Toronto dorm to grey rain and a lab report due. At home in Ahmedabad it was Diwali morning: Ba drawing rangoli, oil lamps on the steps, the smell of mathiya frying. Hansa watched the family video call on mute during class and felt hollow. October 27: she told Gopika, from the same floor, 'I didn't even light a candle.' Gopika admitted she had cried on Onam. November 3: the two of them and their friend Linh made a tiny rangoli from coloured rice on a paper plate, lit battery candles because real flames weren't allowed, and ate shop-bought laddoos. Hansa photographed it for Ba. It wasn't Diwali. But it was something they'd made, and she decided they would do it every year.

qa.q: What did Hansa, Gopika and Linh use to make the rangoli?
qa.a: Coloured rice on a paper plate.

qa.q: What did Hansa feel watching the family call on mute during class?
qa.a: She felt hollow and homesick, missing the Diwali morning rituals at home.

qa.q: What helped Hansa feel more anchored?
qa.a: Sharing the feeling with Gopika and creating a small new ritual together, a rice rangoli and battery candles, that she plans to repeat.

qa.q: How might Gopika relate to Hansa's homesickness?
qa.a: Gopika had cried on Onam, so she understands and is glad to share a new ritual.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Tejas, before you fly to Germany, sit with your Uma athai for a minute. When I was nineteen, I went to a hostel in Lucknow, far from Madurai. Nobody there drew kolam at dawn. Nobody said 'saapdu', eat, the way Amma did, three times, even when you'd already eaten. For the first month I felt like a kite with a cut string. Then one morning I took chalk and drew a small kolam outside my hostel room door. The warden frowned but let it stay. By the end of the year, three other girls on my floor were drawing their own designs beside mine: a star, a lotus, a Bengali alpana. So when you feel lost there, don't wait for home to come to you. Draw your little kolam.

qa.q: What did young Uma draw outside her hostel room door?
qa.a: A small kolam, in chalk.

qa.q: What did young Uma mean by feeling 'like a kite with a cut string'?
qa.a: She felt homesick and unanchored, missing the daily rituals of home.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped young Uma, and how did it spread?
qa.a: Drawing a kolam at her door each morning; it anchored her, and by the end of the year three other girls were drawing their own designs beside hers.

qa.q: How might the three girls on the floor have felt joining in?
qa.a: They likely felt homesick too, and adding a star, a lotus or an alpana let them bring a piece of their own homes into the hostel.

grounding: An aunt recalls missing home rituals in a hostel and creating a small daily one that anchored her and others.

subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage: Kiran, you want your new team to feel like a team? Let old Chetan tell you how it happened, back in 2003, at the printing press. Twelve of us, and nobody talked except to complain. One Friday I bought a flask of cutting chai and a packet of glucose biscuits and put them on the proofing table at four. I said, 'Five minutes, no work talk.' Only two came. The next Friday, five. By the end of the month, the machine operators were bringing their own snacks, and the proofreaders were arguing about cricket with them. We did Friday chai for eleven years. When I left, the youngest apprentice made a speech about it. It was never about the chai.

qa.q: At what time did Chetan put the chai on the proofing table?
qa.a: At four, on Fridays.

qa.q: How might the machine operators have felt by the end of that month?
qa.a: Probably more included and relaxed, bringing their own snacks and arguing about cricket with the proofreaders.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the ritual take hold?
qa.a: Starting small and keeping it every Friday even when only two came, with one simple rule: no work talk.

qa.q: What might the ritual have meant to the youngest apprentice who made the speech?
qa.a: It likely felt like the heart of belonging at the press, which is why the apprentice spoke about it when Chetan left.

grounding: A senior recalls creating a weekly chai ritual that turned a group of workers into a community.

subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage: Harish and Vasudha's first flat in Hyderabad had one gas burner, two plates and very little money left after the rent. Their families had big Sunday lunches back home; here there was no one to cook for but each other. The first two Sundays they ate instant noodles and scrolled their phones in silence, and both felt oddly lonely. On the third Sunday Vasudha said, 'New rule. Sunday is dosa and a walk.' They made lopsided dosas on the one burner, one at a time, taking turns to flip. Then they walked to the lake and each said one good thing about the week. By the second month, their neighbour Salma aunty had started joining the walk, bringing chutney.

qa.q: How many gas burners did the flat have?
qa.a: One.

qa.q: How did Harish and Vasudha feel during the first two Sundays?
qa.a: Oddly lonely, eating instant noodles and scrolling their phones in silence, missing the big family lunches.

qa.q: Why did 'dosa and a walk' work as a new ritual?
qa.a: It was cheap and simple, fitted the one burner, and gave them a regular shared time with one good thing each to say.

qa.q: What might joining the walk mean to Salma aunty?
qa.a: She likely enjoys the company and feels welcomed into their small new tradition, which is why she brings chutney.

grounding: A newly married couple on a tight budget creates a simple weekly ritual that grows into a small community.

subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage: When Sahil took over the design team at a small office in Andheri, the six of them ate lunch at their desks with headphones on. Nobody knew each other's birthdays. Sahil didn't give a speech about culture. Sahil just started 'Wednesday wada pav': at 11:30 every Wednesday, a bag of wada pav from the stall downstairs went on the meeting table, and whoever came, came. Akash, the quietest designer, started bringing a one-question quiz on a sticky note. By the fourth week, Priti from accounts was sneaking over from the next team. When Sahil had to miss a Wednesday for a client visit, Sahil came back to find the team had done it anyway, and had saved one wada pav, now cold.

qa.q: At what time was 'Wednesday wada pav'?
qa.a: At 11:30 every Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt finding the saved, cold wada pav?
qa.a: Likely touched and pleased, seeing the ritual had become the team's own, not just Sahil's.

qa.q: What made this ritual take root without a speech?
qa.a: It was small, regular and optional ('whoever came, came'), and others could add to it, like Akash's quiz.

qa.q: What might the Wednesday ritual mean for Akash?
qa.a: As the quietest designer, the quiz gave Akash a comfortable way to join in and be noticed.

grounding: A new team lead creates a small weekly ritual that turns a group of individuals into a team.

subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage:
Dear Nandini,
You asked how Nani's Milad went. I went. You know I stopped praying years ago, and I almost made an excuse. But I sat in the corner with the women while the naats were recited, and I watched Nani. Her lips moved with every line. Her hands shook when she raised them. My aunt said Nani had waited all year for this, since Nana died.
I didn't pretend to pray. I also didn't roll my eyes like I used to at sixteen. I passed the rose water, served the sheer khurma and held Nani's elbow when she stood. At the end she squeezed my hand and said, 'You came.' That was the whole point, I think.
Love,
Hafsa

qa.q: What did Hafsa serve at the Milad?
qa.a: The sheer khurma; Hafsa also passed the rose water.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling while watching Nani's lips move?
qa.a: Hafsa felt moved and tender, seeing how much the ritual meant to Nani, even without sharing the belief.

qa.q: How did Hafsa take part without pretending?
qa.a: By not faking prayer or mocking it, and instead helping: serving, passing rose water and supporting Nani's elbow.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's presence mean to Nani?
qa.a: Nani had waited all year for the Milad since Nana died, so 'You came' shows she felt comforted and honoured.

grounding: An adult attends a grandmother's religious gathering without sharing the belief, sees what it means to her and takes part respectfully.

subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage: Deepika, fair question for your show. How do non-believers handle family rituals? Okay, this is Harsha. Last month my parents did a griha pravesh for their new flat. I'm not religious, and my cousins know it. Some of them expected me to sulk in a corner. I didn't sit at the fire and chant, because that would have felt like lying. But I watched my father's face when the priest tied the thread on his wrist. He'd worked thirty-five years for that flat. His eyes were wet. So I carried the kalash, handed out the prasad and stood behind him the whole time. My aunt teased me, 'Atheist carrying the kalash!' I said, 'I'm carrying it for Papa.' He heard. He didn't say anything, just patted my arm.

qa.q: What did the priest tie on the father's wrist?
qa.a: The thread.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel watching the father's face?
qa.a: Harsha felt moved and protective, seeing his wet eyes after thirty-five years of work for the flat.

qa.q: How did Harsha show respect without pretending?
qa.a: By not chanting at the fire, which felt like lying, but carrying the kalash, handing out prasad and standing behind Papa.

qa.q: What might Harsha's father have felt when he heard 'I'm carrying it for Papa'?
qa.a: Likely touched and proud, which is why he patted Harsha's arm without words.

grounding: An adult attends a family ritual without belief, sees what it means to a parent and takes part honestly and respectfully.

subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage: I'm Ankita, and I'll just describe what I saw, because I'm still not sure what I felt. Dadi's Satyanarayan katha was in the living room, the sofa pushed back, everyone on the floor. I don't believe in it; my family knows. My brother Hemant, who does, sat right next to the pandit. Dadi's hands trembled as she poured the milk. She had been ill all winter, and it struck me that she might be thinking this could be her last katha. When the story reached the part where the merchant forgets his promise, Dadi looked straight at me and smiled. I didn't fold my hands like Hemant. I sat beside her, kept the lamp from going out and passed the prasad round the room. Afterwards Hemant said, 'You stayed the whole time.' Dadi said nothing, only kept her hand on my knee.

qa.q: What did Ankita keep from going out?
qa.a: The lamp.

qa.q: What might Ankita have been feeling when Dadi looked over and smiled?
qa.a: Ankita seems moved and uncertain, touched by what the katha meant to Dadi without believing in it.

qa.q: How did Ankita take part with respect and honesty?
qa.a: By not folding hands or pretending, but sitting beside Dadi, tending the lamp and passing the prasad.

qa.q: What does the katha seem to mean to Dadi?
qa.a: After a winter of illness it seems deeply important, perhaps a last chance, and having Ankita beside her clearly comforts her.

grounding: An adult who does not share the belief attends a grandmother's ritual, sees what it means to her and takes part without pretending.
